newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe says left can win -- right also.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe says left can win -- right also.

text.p: French conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Thursday the left-wing opposition could win Sunday's parliamentary election runoff after taking a stunning lead in the first round.
Asked in a radio interview if the left could win, the outoing premier said: "Yes. Yes it can win, and everyone must understand that this is what is at stake."
But he added the ruling conservatives could also win in the tight race and denied they were overwhelmed by fear of losing.
"I do not feel this defeatism at all. I have seen the will to win, because we too can win. Victory is within our reach," he said.

Juppe, who has announced he will resign after the election whatever the result, said the electorate had cast a protest vote in the first round but should think carefully before electing a left-wing government and forcing "cohabitation" on conservative Gaullist President Jacques Chirac.

"We will get it for five years and we must think what France will look like in the year 2000 according to whether we have a Socialist-Communist-Green majority or a RPR-UDF majority," said Juppe, leader of the RPR Gaullist party.
Juppe backed a "ticket" of socially-minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin, seen as the coalition's last hope, but his centrist UDF allies criticised it.
Juppe said it would be a good team because the two men were "in agreement on the essentials".
But UDF leader Francois Leotard, a former defence minister, said "you can't be both a liberal skylark and a big piece of Socialist horsemeat. That doesn't work".

Seguin, the outgoing National Assembly speaker and a former anti-Maastricht campaigner, and the liberal ex-finance minister Madelin held a joint election rally on Wednesday as they emerged as the right's improbable saviours with Chirac's blessing.
Leotard condemned power-sharing between Gaullist President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Lionel Jospin if the left wins, and his criticism also applied to a possible Seguin-Madelin team.

"I am simply saying: we have to choose. We have perhaps reached this situation because we have not chosen over the past two years," he said. Chirac appointed Juppe two years ago upon his election as president.
"We need to be coherent. I believe we must be liberal in the world we are in. All the countries around us are liberal," Leotard said.
Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, the former UDF leader, also criticised a Seguin-Madelin team as an operation involving individuals rarther than policies.
"There is no providential man for the ruling coalition. There must be a providential idea: create jobs and restore growth," he told RTL radio.
